title: Where Did the Green Peas Go? Mendel's Hidden Traits and the Coin-Flip Behind Heredity

source.title: Experiments in Plant-Hybridisation
source.authors: Gregor Mendel; W. Bateson, M.A., F.R.S. (introduction, translation and defence)
source.venue: Mendel's Principles of Heredity: A Defence (Cambridge University Press)

intro.summary: This 1902 book reprints Gregor Mendel's 1865 pea experiments, together with Bateson's introduction and his defence of Mendel against the critic W. F. R. Weldon. Mendel asked whether the offspring of crossed plants follow a countable law. He crossed pea varieties that differed in one clear trait and counted thousands of descendants over several generations. He found that a hidden trait comes back in about one plant in four. He explained this by proposing that each pollen grain and each egg carries only one of the two versions of a trait, in equal numbers, and that they pair up by chance. The main limits: the work covers a few sharply defined pea traits. Some cases behave differently, such as Hieracium hybrids that breed true and the colours of Phaseolus beans, and Mendel called parts of his account a hypothesis that still needed confirming. Bateson is an open advocate, so his treatment of Weldon's objections is one side of a live dispute, not a settled verdict. This lesson does not cover in depth Galton's and Pearson's statistical law of ancestry, blending traits like human height, or what physically carries a trait. Those, along with later chromosome theory, are good topics to follow up.
background: A pea plant usually fertilises itself: pollen from its own flower lands on its own egg cells, so a breeder must open the bud and remove the pollen-making parts to cross two plants by hand.
A 'variety' that breeds true gives offspring that all look like itself, generation after generation.
Before Mendel, many people assumed that a parent's traits blend in its children, the way mixing red and white paint makes pink.
In 1902 nobody knew what physical thing in a cell carries a trait. Genes and chromosomes had not yet been linked to heredity.
intro.aha: A trait can vanish completely in one generation and then return, unchanged, in almost exactly one plant out of four, because every pollen grain and egg carries only one version of the trait and chance pairing does the rest.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Gardeners had crossed plants for a century. They knew that the offspring of a cross, called hybrids, often look like one parent, and that later generations come out mixed. Nobody had a law that predicted how many of each kind would appear. Mendel thought the earlier experiments had simply not counted carefully enough.
primer.quote: not one has been carried out to such an extent and in such a way as to make it possible to determine the number of different forms under which the offspring of hybrids appear

primer.heading: What Mendel did
primer.body: He tested pea varieties for two years and kept only those that bred true. He then crossed varieties that differed in one clear-cut trait, such as round versus wrinkled seeds or yellow versus green seeds. He let the hybrids fertilise themselves and sorted and counted every seed and plant, for up to six generations. In total he examined more than 10,000 plants.
primer.quote: In all, thirty-four more or less distinct varieties of Peas were obtained from several seedsmen and subjected to a two years’ trial.
primer.quote_where: Mendel, Selection of the Experimental Plants

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: The first hybrids all looked like one parent. Mendel called that trait 'dominant' and the hidden one 'recessive'. In the next generation the hidden trait came back unchanged in about one plant in four, for all seven traits. Single plants varied a lot, but the large totals were close to 3 to 1. Later tests showed the 3 to 1 split is really 1 pure-dominant : 2 hybrid : 1 pure-recessive. Mendel explained this by germ cells (pollen and eggs) that each carry only one version, made in equal numbers and paired by chance.
primer.quote: If now the results of the whole of the experiments be brought together, there is found, as between the number of forms with the dominant and recessive characters, an average ratio of 2·98 to 1, or 3 to 1.
primer.quote_where: Mendel, The First Generation from the Hybrids

primer.heading: Why it matters, and the argument it started
primer.body: Galton's popular 'law of ancestral heredity' said every grandparent and great-grandparent shares in a child's makeup. Bateson argues that Mendel's result breaks that idea. A green pea pulled out of a hybrid family breeds as purely green as one that was never crossed. In 1902 the critic Weldon replied that Mendel had ignored ancestry and that exceptions exist. Bateson answers that dominance was never Mendel's law and that the real discovery is the purity of the germ cells.
primer.quote: Mendel’s conception differs fundamentally from that involved in the Law of Ancestral Heredity.

primer.heading: The limits
primer.body: Mendel used only traits with a sharp either-or difference. He set aside traits that differ 'more or less'. His later work on Hieracium found hybrids that breed true, the opposite of peas, and his bean flower colours did not fit simply. Even Bateson admits that a few real exceptions remain in peas and that absolute purity of germ cells is not proven. Mendel himself asked for the key experiments to be repeated.
primer.quote: Even the validity of the law formulated for Pisum requires still to be confirmed, and a repetition of the more important experiments is consequently much to be desired

concepts.title: The hybrid looks like just one parent
concepts.idea: When two true-breeding pea varieties are crossed, the hybrid shows one parent's trait in full and the other trait seems to vanish, instead of the two blending.

terms.means: A variety whose seeds always grow into plants just like the parent, year after year
The idea that a child's trait is a mix of its parents' traits, like stirring two paints together
Mendel's name for the parent's feature that shows in full in the hybrid
Mendel's name for the parent's feature that seems to disappear (becomes 'latent') in the hybrid

concepts.recap: In Mendel's chosen pea crosses, the hybrid copied one parent's feature in full; the other feature was hidden, not mixed away.

understand.explanation: Mendel first grew 34 pea varieties for two years and kept those that were true-breeding: each one's seeds always gave plants like the parent. He then crossed varieties that differed in one sharp, either-or feature, such as yellow versus green seeds. If heredity worked by blending, the hybrid seeds should have come out yellow-green, halfway between. Instead, in all seven of his crosses the hybrid looked like one parent, and the other parent's feature could not be seen. He called the feature that shows dominant and the one that hides recessive, and it made no difference which parent gave the pollen. This is an observation about his chosen peas, not a law for every trait: he deliberately left out 'more or less' features, his tall × dwarf hybrids were even taller than the tall parent, and Bateson notes crosses, such as a magenta × white primrose, that do give an in-between colour.
understand.quote: Henceforth in this paper those characters which are transmitted entire, or almost unchanged in the hybridisation, and therefore in themselves constitute the characters of the hybrid, are termed the dominant, and those which become latent in the process recessive.
understand.quote_where: Mendel, 'Experiments in Plant-Hybridisation', section 'The Forms of the Hybrids'

activities.question: Take a pea variety whose seeds are always yellow inside and another whose seeds are always green inside. You dust the pollen of one onto the flowers of the other. What do you expect the seeds of this cross to look like?

options.feedback: This is the 'mixing' guess: children as an average of their parents, like stirring two paints. Many naturalists of Mendel's day thought this way. Keep your guess in mind; the next screens show what Mendel actually counted.
This guess says one parent's colour wins completely. Hold on to it; you will check it against Mendel's report in a moment.
This guess also says one colour wins completely, but picks green. Keep it in mind; you will see which colour Mendel reported.

options.text: A mixture: some seeds yellow, some green
options.feedback: This guess says each seed goes one way or the other. That is a sharp idea, and it matters later in the lesson. For now, hold on to it and see what Mendel found in this first cross.

activities.prompt: Three ways two parents could combine. Which one did Mendel's pea crosses look like?

cases.label: What blending predicts
cases.text: If heredity worked like mixing paint, yellow × green would give yellow-green seeds. Once mixed, neither pure colour could show up again in the hybrid. This is an everyday comparison, not data from the paper.

cases.label: Mendel's peas
cases.text: In each of his seven crosses, the hybrid resembled one parent so closely that the other parent's feature 'either escapes observation completely or cannot be detected with certainty'. Yellow × green gave yellow seeds, whichever plant gave the pollen.

cases.label: A blend the paper does mention
cases.text: Bateson's introduction describes a cross between a rich crimson magenta Chinese Primrose and a clear white one, giving 'a flower of a colour appropriately described as a "washy" magenta'. So real in-between hybrids do exist for some traits.

activities.takeaway: Mendel's pea features behaved like the middle case: one parent's feature showed in full and the other went out of sight. Bateson stresses that this is true of particular traits and varieties, not a universal rule, since the primrose shows a genuine blend.

activities.title: Which feature shows in the hybrid?
activities.prompt: Mendel crossed pea varieties that differed in one feature at a time. Sort each feature: does it show in the hybrid, or does it hide? Watch out: the same colour can be on different sides for different parts of the plant.

cards.feedback: Round seeds show. Mendel lists 'the round or roundish form of the seed' among the dominant features.
Wrinkled hides. A round × wrinkled hybrid makes round seeds, sometimes with shallow dents, but not wrinkled ones.

cards.text: Yellow seed colour (the inside of the seed)
cards.feedback: Yellow shows for seed colour. The seed coat was clear, so Mendel could see the yellow inside directly.

cards.text: Green seed colour (the inside of the seed)
cards.feedback: Green hides for seed colour, so yellow × green gives yellow seeds and not a yellow-green blend.
Green shows here. For the colour of the unripe pod, Mendel lists the green colouring as dominant, the opposite of seed colour.
Yellow hides here. Being yellow does not make a feature dominant: which side wins depends on the particular feature, not on the colour name.
Long stem shows, with a twist: Mendel found the hybrid usually grew even taller than the long parent (6 to 7½ ft from 1 ft × 6 ft parents), not halfway between.
Short stem hides. The hybrid is tall, not medium, so this is not a blend either.

activities.takeaway: In all seven of Mendel's crosses one feature showed and the other hid. The other three dominant features were grey-brown seed coats with violet-red flowers, simply inflated pods, and flowers spread along the stem. Which side wins is a fact about each feature, and the long-stem case shows the hybrid can even go beyond its showing parent. Where the hidden feature goes is the next question.

concepts.title: The hidden trait returns: 3 to 1, but only in big counts
concepts.idea: When hybrids fertilise themselves, about one offspring in four shows the hidden trait, and that share only settles near 1/4 when many seeds are counted.

predict.question: Mendel ran several 3-to-1 experiments of very different sizes. In one he counted 8,023 seeds for seed colour. In another he counted only 580 plants for pod colour. Which result would you expect to land farther from exactly 3 to 1?
options: Both equally close, because the same rule governs both
Neither: a real rule always gives exactly 3 to 1
why: Right. A smaller count has a wider band of chance results. Mendel's pod-colour count gave 2.82 to 1, the largest departure among his seven experiments, while 8,023 seeds gave 3.01 to 1.
A big count might seem to have more room for error. In fact more seeds shrink the band, so 8,023 seeds should land closest to 1 in 4, and it did, at 3.01 to 1.
The rule is the same, but the rule only sets the average. How far a count strays depends on how many seeds or plants were counted, and 580 is far fewer than 8,023.
This treats 3 to 1 as a promise for every count. It is an average: any finite count wobbles around it, and smaller counts wobble more.

terms.means: How many seeds (or plants) you count before working out a share
How far a count strays from the expected share purely through luck in which seeds happened to form
To halve the spread of a count's likely results you need four times as many seeds, not twice as many

model.title: Where the share of green seeds is likely to land
model.note: Teaching model. Each seed from a self-fertilised hybrid is treated as an independent 1-in-4 chance of being green. The curve uses the bell-shaped approximation to that chance, which is rough for a single plant. Each plant is taken to give 31 seeds, Mendel's average (8,023 seeds from 258 plants in his seed-colour experiment). Real plants vary in seed number, and Mendel warns that faint green seeds are easy to miscount. The marked counts (1 of 33, 19 of 39, and 2,001 of 8,023 green) are Mendel's own data. The curve and the shaded band are illustrative.

x.label: Share of seeds that are green

steps.say: This curve shows where the share of green seeds is likely to land when you count seeds from hybrid pea plants.
This line marks one in four, the share Mendel found on average.
This slider sets how many plants' seeds you count. Each plant gives about 31 seeds.
The shaded band is where 95 of every 100 counts would fall. Watch it squeeze as you count more plants.
These two lines are real single plants from Mendel's notebook, and this one is his grand total.

explore.prompt: You are planning a count. Use the slider to find how much counting it takes before chance stops hiding the 1-in-4 pattern.

goals.text: Find the fewest plants that keep 95 of every 100 counts between 20% and 30% green
hints: The band is symmetric around one in four, so watch just one of its edges.
Move the slider up slowly from one plant and stop the moment the low edge clears 20%.
It takes a handful of plants: more than five, fewer than fifteen.

goals.text: Make the band a quarter as wide as it is for a single plant
hints: Recall from the walkthrough what it took to make the band half as wide.
Halving the band needs four times the seeds, not twice.
A quarter is half of a half, so apply that four-times rule twice, starting from one plant.

feedback.correct: Yes. The 3-to-1 rule fixes the average, but how far a count strays depends on its size. Mendel's smallest experiments wandered most: pod colour, with 580 plants, gave 2.82 to 1.
feedback.incorrect: You may have read 3 to 1 as a promise that every count hits. It is an average over many seeds. Small counts swing widely around it and big counts hug it, so the 580-plant pod-colour count was the one most likely to stray, and it did (2.82 to 1).

steps.say: Start with one plant, about 31 seeds. The band runs from roughly 10% to 40% green. That spread comes from luck alone, because each seed is a fresh draw. We call this chance fluctuation.
Mendel saw exactly this. One hybrid plant gave 20 yellow and 19 green seeds, nearly half. Another gave 32 yellow and just 1 green. Single plants are poor witnesses to the rule.
Now count four plants, about 124 seeds. The number you count is the sample size. With four times the seeds, the band is about half as wide.
Quadruple again, to 16 plants: the band halves again. This is the square-root rule. Every halving of the spread costs four times the counting.
At 100 plants, about 3,100 seeds, nearly every count lands between about 23.5% and 26.5% green. Luck now has little room to hide the pattern.

This is Mendel's seed-colour experiment: 258 plants, 8,023 seeds. The band is under two points wide, and his real total, 2,001 green (24.9%), sits right beside one in four. That is a ratio of 3.01 to 1.
So the hidden trait really does return in about one seed in four, but you can only see that clearly in a big crowd of seeds, never in one pod or one plant.

understand.explanation: When Mendel let his hybrid peas fertilise themselves, the hidden trait (such as green seed colour) came back in about one seed in four, or 3 dominant to 1 hidden. But the 1/4 is an average, not a promise for any single plant. Each seed behaves like a separate lucky draw, so one plant's count can swing widely: Mendel recorded 20 yellow to 19 green on one plant, and 32 yellow to 1 green on another. Added up over 258 plants, his 8,023 seeds gave 6,022 yellow to 2,001 green (3.01 to 1), and his seven experiments together averaged 2.98 to 1. His smaller experiments strayed more (pod colour, 580 plants, gave 2.82 to 1), which is why he insisted the true ratio needs big totals. Two caveats remain. Mendel warns that faint green seeds are easy to miscount. Bateson later judged the numbers, though large, 'not large enough to give really smooth results'.
understand.quote: The true ratios of the numbers can only be ascertained by an average deduced from the sum of as many single values as possible; the greater the number the more are merely chance elements eliminated.
understand.quote_where: Mendel, Experiments in Plant-Hybridisation, section 'The Reproductive Cells of Hybrids' (p. 75 of Bateson's 1902 edition)

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's rule, not an equation from the paper. Mendel's own result is the average share of 1/4, the ratio 3 : 1. N is the number of seeds counted (31 × plants), the blue output, and the width is the green output. Because N sits under a square root, four times the seeds makes the band half as wide.

concepts.recap: The hidden trait comes back in about one seed in four, but only a big count reveals that 3 to 1. One plant can stray far by chance alone.

activities.question: In his seed-colour experiment Mendel counted 8,023 seeds from hybrid plants, and 2,001 of them were green. Roughly what percentage of the seeds were green?
activities.explanation: 2,001 ÷ 8,023 ≈ 0.249, almost exactly one in four. The other 6,022 were yellow, a ratio of 3.01 to 1. With this many seeds, chance can only nudge the share by about a point.
hints: Divide the green seeds by all the seeds.
2,000 out of 8,000 would be exactly a quarter.

activities.question: One single hybrid plant in the same experiment gave 20 yellow and 19 green seeds. What percentage of that plant's seeds were green?
activities.explanation: 19 ÷ 39 ≈ 0.49, nearly half, far from one in four. Mendel listed it as an extreme. With only 39 seeds, chance alone can push one plant's count a long way from the average.
hints: Add the two counts to get the plant's total seeds.
19 out of 39 is a little under half.

concepts.title: Not all yellows are alike: 1 pure to 2 hybrid
concepts.idea: Breeding on the dominant-looking plants shows that one third breed true while two thirds split 3 to 1 again, so the 3:1 is really 1:2:1.

terms.means: A plant breeds true when every offspring it makes by fertilising itself shows the same trait it shows
Among the hybrids' offspring: 1 true-breeding dominant plant, then 2 hybrids that only look dominant, then 1 recessive plant

concepts.recap: Yellow peas from hybrids come in two hidden kinds, 1 true-breeding for every 2 hybrids, so the 3 : 1 is really 1 : 2 : 1.

understand.explanation: Every yellow pea grown from a hybrid's seeds looks the same, so Mendel told them apart by their offspring. He grew each one, let it fertilise itself, and checked all of its seeds. A plant breeds true when all its offspring match it, and about one third of the yellow plants did: they gave only yellow seeds. The other two thirds gave yellow and green seeds in about 3 to 1, just like the original hybrids. So the familiar 3 yellow : 1 green hides three kinds of plant in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio: 1 true-breeding yellow, 2 hybrids that only look yellow, and 1 green. His largest counts came near 2 hybrids to 1 true-breeder (for example 353 to 166), while smaller tests of 100 plants wandered further, as he said was to be expected.
understand.quote: Of these two-thirds yield offspring which display the dominant and recessive characters in the proportion of 3 to 1, and thereby show exactly the same ratio as the hybrid forms, while only one-third remains with the dominant character constant.
understand.quote_where: Mendel, 'Experiments in Plant-Hybridisation', section 'The Second Generation [Bred] from the Hybrids'

activities.title: Turning Mendel's counts into 1 : 2 : 1

steps.text: Start where the last idea ended. The hybrids fertilised themselves and gave about 3 yellow seeds for every 1 green. 'Yellow' here means the colour inside the seed, the trait that showed in the hybrid.
Mendel grew 519 plants from these yellow seeds (his Experiment 2). Each plant fertilised itself, and he looked at that plant's seeds on their own.
steps.result: 519 yellow-looking plants tested one by one

steps.text: 166 plants gave only yellow seeds. Each of these breeds true: it behaves like a pure yellow variety.
353 plants gave both yellow and green seeds, again in about 3 to 1. They behave exactly like the hybrids they came from, even though they look yellow.
Compare the two groups: 353 ÷ 166 ≈ 2.13. For seed shape (Experiment 1) the split was 372 to 193, about 1.93. Together they average almost exactly 2 to 1.

The green plants were tested too. They gave only green seeds and never changed. So every 4 offspring of a hybrid sort into 1 true-breeding yellow, 2 hybrids and 1 true-breeding green. Mendel wrote this as A + 2Aa + a.

A caution from the paper: for five other traits he tested only 100 plants, with 10 seeds each. Those results ranged from 60 : 40 to 72 : 28. When he repeated the most uneven one, 60 : 40 became 65 : 35. Small samples drift.

activities.takeaway: The 3 : 1 you see is a 1 : 2 : 1 you can't see. Only the next generation reveals which yellow plants are pure and which are hybrids.

activities.prompt: Put Mendel's steps in order, from the first cross to the test that split the yellow plants into two kinds.
items: Cross a true-breeding yellow pea with a true-breeding green pea
The hybrid seeds all look yellow
The hybrids fertilise themselves: about 3 yellow seeds to 1 green
Grow each yellow seed into a plant and let it fertilise itself
About one third give only yellow; two thirds give yellow and green about 3 to 1
activities.explanation: The two kinds of yellow only show up one generation after the 3 : 1. You cannot tell a pure yellow from a hybrid yellow by looking. You have to let each plant breed and examine its own offspring.
hints: Which step has to happen before any hybrid exists?
The 3 : 1 count comes before the test of individual yellow plants, because that test uses the yellow seeds from the 3 : 1.

activities.question: Mendel lets these plants fertilise themselves. Which group will never again give green seeds, at least within the generations he followed?

options.text: The one third of yellow plants that bred true
options.feedback: Right. Their seeds were all yellow, and Mendel reports that these pure dominants stayed constant in later generations. He carried some experiments through six generations. Bateson later noted that rare stray pollen or new variation can still upset a line.

options.text: The two thirds of yellow plants that gave yellow and green 3 to 1
options.feedback: These are hybrids in disguise. They already produced green seeds, about one in four, and their yellow offspring split again in the same way.
The green plants do breed true, but they breed true to green. The question asks which plants never produce the green form, and these produce nothing else.

options.text: All the yellow plants, since they look identical
options.feedback: Looks are the trap here. The yellow plants look alike, but breeding them showed two kinds, and the hybrid kind keeps producing green seeds.

hints: Ask what each group's own seeds looked like when it fertilised itself.
Only one group of yellow plants gave seeds of a single colour.

concepts.title: One version per pollen grain, paired by chance
concepts.idea: If a hybrid makes pollen and eggs that each carry only one version, half of each kind, then random pairing gives 1 pure : 2 hybrid : 1 pure, which looks like 3 to 1.

predict.question: Mendel also crossed hybrids with pure plants. Say a pure yellow plant supplies the eggs, so every egg carries yellow. A hybrid supplies the pollen: half its grains carry yellow and half carry green, one version each. They pair by chance. What offspring should you expect?
options: About half pure yellow and half hybrid, with no green at all
1 pure yellow : 2 hybrid : 1 pure green, as before
Three yellow-looking plants to every green one
why: Right. Every egg brings yellow, so no plant can get two greens. Yellow pollen makes pure yellows and green pollen makes hybrids, about 1 to 1, and every plant looks yellow.
Tempting, because that is the hybrid-by-hybrid result. But 1:2:1 needs both the pollen and the eggs split half and half. Here the eggs are all yellow, so the green-with-green box stays empty.
3 to 1 is how 1:2:1 looks to the eye. You only get it when green can come from both sides. These eggs never carry green, so no green plants appear.
You would get all hybrids only if every pollen grain carried green. Half the grains here carry yellow, and with all-yellow eggs those make pure yellow plants.

terms.means: A germ cell, meaning a pollen grain or an egg. One of each joins to start a new plant.
Bateson's name for Mendel's idea that each germ cell carries only one version of a trait, never a mix of both
Bateson's word for a plant formed from two unlike germ cells, such as yellow pollen with a green egg. This is the hybrid.

model.title: Pairing a hybrid's pollen with its eggs
model.note: Teaching model: one trait (seed colour) with two versions. Each box is the share of offspring you would expect if pollen and eggs met purely at random, with no counting luck. Real counts wobble around these shares, as in the earlier concept. The 'mix' switch is a simplified stand-in for the blending view. Shares are idealised, not Mendel's counts.

controls.label: Every pollen grain and egg carries a mix of both

steps.say: This grid pairs a hybrid pea's pollen (columns) with its eggs (rows). Each box shows how many of every 100 offspring come from that pairing.
This slider sets how much of the pollen carries the yellow version. The rest carries green.
This one does the same for the eggs.
This switch tries a rival idea: every grain carries a mix of both versions.
These boxes add up the offspring: pure yellow, hybrid and pure green.

explore.prompt: You have seen the even split give 1:2:1. Now look for other ways the grid can make green plants, and see what each way changes.

goals.text: Find another way to get one green offspring in four. Keep mixing off, and split the pollen and the eggs differently from each other. Then look at the pure-yellow box.
hints: A green plant needs green from the pollen AND green from the egg, so the two green shares multiply.
What if every pollen grain carried green? Then the green box is just the share of eggs that carry green.
Slide the pollen all the way to green, then move the egg slider until the green box reads one in four.

feedback.correct: Yes. With every egg carrying yellow, the green-egg row is empty. Yellow pollen gives pure yellows and green pollen gives hybrids, about 1 to 1, and all of them look yellow.
feedback.incorrect: You may have carried over the 1:2:1 from a hybrid fertilising itself. The grid gives 1:2:1 only when both the pollen and the eggs are split half and half. Here every egg carries yellow, so no plant can be pure green.

steps.say: Start with every pollen grain and every egg carrying yellow. Only one box fills: all 100 offspring are pure yellow. That is a true-breeding yellow plant, not a hybrid.
Mendel's idea: each pollen grain or egg a hybrid makes, called a gamete, keeps one version, never both. Bateson called this the purity of the gametes. Split the pollen half yellow, half green.
Split the eggs evenly too. Now there are four pairings, each equally likely by chance, so each box gets 25 of every 100 offspring.
Two boxes pair unlike versions: yellow pollen with a green egg, and green pollen with a yellow egg. Both make the same hybrid, which Bateson called a heterozygote. Together that is 50.
Add it up: 25 pure yellow, 50 hybrid, 25 pure green. That is 1 : 2 : 1, the split the breeding test in the last concept uncovered.
The hybrids look yellow, so to the eye it is 75 yellow to 25 green. That is the 3 to 1.
Try the rival blending idea: every grain carries a mix. Every offspring is mix with mix, and pure green can never come back. Yet Mendel saw pure greens return.
Switch back. One version per gamete, half of each kind, paired by chance, and the 1 : 2 : 1 returns, green plants included.

understand.explanation: Mendel proposed that a hybrid's pollen grains and eggs each carry just one version of a trait, yellow or green, never both, and that it makes the two kinds in equal numbers. If pollen and eggs then meet at random, the four pairings happen about equally often. That gives one pure yellow, two hybrids and one pure green. Because hybrids look yellow, this 1:2:1 shows up as 3 to 1. Mendel worked backwards from his counts to this idea and then tested it with further crosses. The idea concerns averages: single pods and plants vary by chance. Bateson also noted cases, such as traits showing different strengths, that the simple purity idea does not yet explain.
understand.quote: the results are such as we might expect if it be imagined that the cross-bred plant produced pollen grains and egg-cells, each of which bears only one of the alternative varietal characters and not both. If this were so, and if on an average the same number of pollen grains and egg-cells transmit each of the two characters, it is clear that on a random assortment of pollen grains and egg-cells Mendel’s law would be obeyed.
understand.quote_where: Bateson's introduction, 'The Problems of Heredity and their Solution'

check.task: Put the model in the state Mendel's idea predicts for a hybrid fertilising itself: green comes back in one plant in four, and the yellow-looking plants split 1 pure to 2 hybrid.
check.hint: Can a mixed grain ever make a pure green plant? Then think about how the pollen and the eggs must each be split so that every pairing is equally likely.
check.misconception: A hybrid passes on a blend: each of its pollen grains and eggs carries a mix of both versions. If that were true, pure green plants could never reappear among its offspring.

connect.caption: Mendel writes each offspring as pollen over egg, with A for the yellow version and a for the green. A/a means yellow pollen met a green egg. With half of each kind of pollen and egg, the four pairings are equally likely and add up to Mendel's series A + 2Aa + a: pure yellow (A, the yellow output), two hybrids (2Aa, the hybrid output) and pure green (a, the green output). The paper's printed fractions are garbled in this text, so the left side is written in its intended form.

concepts.recap: One version per germ cell, half of each kind, paired by chance gives 1 pure : 2 hybrid : 1 pure, which looks like 3 to 1.

concepts.title: Testing the idea: cross the hybrid with the recessive
concepts.idea: Crossing a hybrid with a pure recessive should give hybrid and recessive offspring in equal numbers, and Mendel's counts in both directions (pollen and egg) confirmed it.

terms.means: Crossing a plant whose make-up is unknown with a pure recessive plant, so that the offspring's looks reveal which versions the unknown plant passed on
The same cross done both ways round: once with plant X as the pollen parent, once with X as the egg parent

model.title: Pairing pollen with eggs
model.note: Teaching model: one trait (seed colour) with two versions. Pollen and eggs may now come from two different plants. Each box is the share of offspring you would expect if pollen and eggs met purely at random, with no counting luck. Real counts wobble around these shares. The 'mix' switch is a simplified stand-in for the blending view. Shares are idealised, not Mendel's data. His real counts appear only in the text, which says where each one comes from.

controls.label: Every pollen grain and egg carries a mix of both

steps.say: This is the same grid as before. Pollen kinds run across the top and egg kinds run down the side. Each box shows the share of offspring from that pairing. Right now it shows a hybrid fertilising itself.
What's new is that the pollen and the eggs can come from two different plants. Drag the egg slider down to zero and every egg carries green, just as a pure green plant's eggs would.
The boxes on the right count what comes out. Keep an eye on the pure green box as the parents change.

explore.prompt: You are Mendel now. Set up the checks he ran, crossing a hybrid with a pure green plant both ways round, and see what the grid predicts.

goals.text: Set up a cross where the hybrid is the egg parent and a pure green plant gives the pollen, with no blending.
hints: Decide which slider stands for the hybrid parent here, and which stands for the green one.
The eggs come from the hybrid, so the egg slider should match a hybrid's eggs. The pollen slider should match a plant that has no yellow version at all.
From the last concept: a hybrid makes its two kinds of eggs in equal numbers. A pure green plant makes only one kind of pollen.

goals.text: Now run the same test the other way round. The hybrid gives the pollen and the pure green plant gives the eggs. Check that the offspring still split evenly.
hints: Swap the roles of the two sliders from the last goal.
The pollen slider now describes the hybrid. The egg slider describes the pure green plant.
A hybrid splits its pollen evenly between its two kinds, the same way it splits its eggs.

predict.question: Imagine a gardener (a made-up case) with a yellow-seeded pea. She doesn't know whether it is pure yellow or a hybrid. She crosses it with a pure green plant and gets 40 seeds, all yellow. What is the best reading?
options: It is almost certainly pure yellow
It is almost certainly a hybrid
The cross tells her nothing, because yellow hides green
why: Right. A hybrid would pass green to about half its offspring, so some green seeds should appear. Forty yellows in a row from a hybrid would be extraordinarily bad luck. That is very unlikely, though not strictly impossible.
You might pick this because hybrids look yellow too. But a hybrid crossed with pure green should give roughly half green seeds, and none appeared.
Yellow does hide green inside one plant. But the green parent supplies only green, so any green version from the unknown plant would show up as a green seed. That is exactly why this cross is a test.
Blending would give in-between seeds, not clear yellow ones. The result is simply what a plant with only yellow versions to give would produce.

feedback.correct: Yes. In a test cross the green parent adds nothing that could hide a green version, so a hybrid would show itself through green seeds. With 40 seeds and no greens, 'pure yellow' is by far the best explanation, though chance can never be ruled out completely.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed that yellow always hides green, so nothing can be learned. In this cross, though, the other parent gives only green versions. Every green version the unknown plant passes on therefore shows up as a green seed. A hybrid would give about half green. All-yellow points to a pure yellow plant.

steps.say: Start where the last concept ended: a hybrid fertilising itself. About a quarter of the offspring are pure yellow, half are hybrid and a quarter are pure green. Yet pure yellow and hybrid offspring look exactly alike.

That is the snag. You can't see pollen or eggs directly. So how could anyone check that a hybrid really makes half yellow and half green? Mendel's answer was to pair the hybrid with a plant that adds nothing to hide: a pure green one.

The green plant's eggs all carry green. So each offspring's look reports its pollen grain: yellow-looking means yellow pollen, green means green. The grid predicts half hybrid, half pure green. This is called a test cross.

That run tested the hybrid's pollen. To test its eggs, swap roles: the hybrid gives the eggs and the green plant gives the pollen. The prediction is the same even split. Doing a cross both ways is called reciprocal crosses.

Compare the blending view. If every pollen grain and egg carried a mix, this same cross would give only mixed offspring and not one pure green seed. The two ideas predict clearly different things, so this is a real test.
Mendel ran this cross. Hybrid eggs with recessive pollen gave seeds in four shape-and-colour kinds: 31, 26, 27 and 26. Adding by colour ourselves: 58 yellow, 52 green. That is close to half and half.

understand.explanation: The 1 : 2 : 1 story makes a sharp prediction you can check. Cross a hybrid with a pure recessive (green) plant, and half the offspring should be hybrids that look yellow while half should be pure green. Mendel did this both ways round. With the hybrid as egg parent (his 2nd experiment) he was testing its eggs, and he reports seeds of four shape-and-colour kinds in numbers 31, 26, 27 and 26. With the hybrid as pollen parent (his 4th experiment) he was testing its pollen, and the four kinds came out as 24, 25, 22 and 27. If we add these up by colour alone (our own sums, not totals printed in the paper), we get 58 yellow to 52 green and 46 yellow to 52 green. Both are near 1 : 1 but not exact, as chance predicts with about a hundred seeds each. The blending view predicts no pure greens at all, so these counts back the idea that each pollen grain and egg carries just one version, made in equal numbers by both sexes.
understand.quote: In all the experiments, therefore, there appeared all the forms which the proposed theory demands, and also in nearly equal numbers.
understand.quote_where: Mendel, 'Experiments in Plant-Hybridisation', section 'The Reproductive Cells of Hybrids'

activities.question: Which passage reports Mendel's test of the hybrid's eggs (hybrid crossed with the pure recessive plant), with counts close to equal?

options.quote: In the 2nd Experiment, 31 round and yellow, 26 round and green, 27 angular and yellow, 26 angular and green seeds.
options.feedback: Yes. This is the hybrid's eggs fertilised by pollen from the pure recessive plant. Adding by colour alone (our sums): 31 + 27 = 58 yellow and 26 + 26 = 52 green, close to half and half.

options.quote: Among them were 5,474 round or roundish ones and 1,850 angular wrinkled ones.
options.feedback: These are real counts, but they come from hybrids fertilising themselves. That gives about 3 to 1, not the even split a test cross predicts.

options.quote: Of these two-thirds yield offspring which display the dominant and recessive characters in the proportion of 3 to 1
options.feedback: This is the earlier finding that two thirds of the yellow-looking plants are hybrids. It concerns self-fertilised plants, not a cross with the recessive.

hints: Look for a cross with the pure recessive form, and add up the seeds by colour alone.

connect.caption: Bateson's notation from his 1902 Defence. D is the dominant version (yellow) and R the recessive one (green). DR is the hybrid, which looks yellow and matches the 'Hybrid offspring' box. RR is the pure green plant, which matches the 'Pure green offspring' box. Bateson writes that Mendel, crossing the hybrids with the pure recessive reciprocally, obtained this ratio.

concepts.recap: Hybrid × pure recessive gives about half and half, whichever parent gives the pollen. So the hybrid's pollen and eggs each carry one version, in equal numbers.

concepts.title: Two traits shuffle separately: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1
concepts.idea: When a hybrid differs in two traits, each trait splits on its own, so the four germ-cell kinds pair at random into a 9:3:3:1 pattern of looks.

predict.question: Mendel also crossed peas that differed in three traits at once: seed shape, seed colour and seed-coat colour. Each trait splits 3 : 1 on its own. In the hybrid's offspring, what share should show all three hidden versions together?
why: 1 in 4 is the share for one trait alone. When three traits sort separately, the shares multiply, so the share for all three together is much smaller.
1 in 12 comes from multiplying 4 by 3, the number of traits. The rule multiplies the shares themselves: ¼ × ¼ × ¼.
1 in 16 is the answer for two traits (¼ × ¼). A third trait that sorts on its own cuts that by another factor of four.

Each hidden version turns up in ¼ of offspring, independently of the others, so all three appear together in ¼ × ¼ × ¼ = 1 in 64. Mendel wrote that such a form would appear 'only once even in sixty-four plants'.

terms.means: Each trait's version goes into a germ cell without regard to which version of another trait goes with it (the modern name for Mendel's 'independent' behaviour)
Mendel's name for the full list of offspring kinds you get by combining the single-trait series (A + 2Aa + a) for each trait

model.title: Four kinds of seed from a round-yellow × wrinkled-green hybrid
model.note: Teaching model: each trait shows its hidden version in a set share of seeds, and every pairing of pollen and egg is equally likely. It ignores chance differences between pods and plants, so the coloured bars are expected shares, not real counts, and are illustrative. The 'glue' switch is an invented comparison, not something Mendel saw. The bars switched on by 'Show Mendel's seeds' are his real counts: 315, 101, 108 and 32 of 556 seeds (his first two-trait experiment).

controls.label: How often seeds come out wrinkled
How often seeds come out green

steps.say: Each bar is one kind of seed a hybrid pea can make: round or wrinkled, yellow or green. Right now every seed is round and yellow.
This slider sets how often a seed comes out wrinkled. Watch seeds move into the wrinkled bars.
This one sets how often a seed comes out green.
This switch glues shape and colour together, so they always travel as a pair. Two bars go empty.
And this switch puts Mendel's own seed counts next to the model.

explore.prompt: Use the rule you just watched, that each trait splits on its own, to predict crosses Mendel really made, and one he never could have seen.

goals.text: Mendel crossed the round-yellow hybrid with a pure wrinkled-green plant and got all four seed types in near-equal numbers (31, 26, 27, 26). Make the unglued model predict that.
hints: Think about one trait at a time. What happens to shape when one parent can only pass on the hidden (wrinkled) version?
Remember the single-trait test with a pure recessive: the dominant and hidden looks came out in equal numbers. Each slider should copy that split.
Give shape and colour the same setting, the share of hidden-look offspring from that single-trait test. All four model bars will then be the same height.

goals.text: Imagine shape and colour glued together in each germ cell. Show a self-fertilised hybrid's seeds then, with each hidden version returning as often as in a single-trait cross.
hints: Which control makes the two traits travel as a pair?
Once they are glued, only the shape slider matters and the two middle bars stay empty. Seeds are either round-yellow or wrinkled-green.
Set the shape slider to the share of hidden-look seeds from the single-trait 3 : 1 split. 'Kinds of seed that appear' should read 2.

feedback.correct: Right. Each trait shows its hidden version in ¼ of offspring regardless of the others, so the shares multiply: ¼ × ¼ × ¼ = 1/64. That is the same multiplying that turned two 3 : 1 splits into 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
feedback.incorrect: You may have used the share for one or two traits, or added instead of multiplied. When traits sort independently, the chance of all three hidden versions together is the product of the separate chances: ¼ × ¼ × ¼ = 1 in 64.

steps.say: Start with one trait. Only shape splits here: wrinkled comes back in 1 seed out of 4 and round in 3. This is the 3 : 1 you already know.
Now let colour split as well, on its own. A quarter of the round seeds turn green, and so does a quarter of the wrinkled ones. Colour ignores shape.
Read the counts out of 16: round-yellow 9, wrinkled-yellow 3, round-green 3, wrinkled-green 1. These are ¾ × ¾, ¼ × ¾, ¾ × ¼ and ¼ × ¼. Two separate 3 : 1 splits multiply into 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

This is independent assortment. Each germ cell gets a shape version and a colour version without one choice affecting the other. That makes four kinds of germ cell in equal numbers, and they pair at random.
Compare what would happen if the traits were glued together. Only two kinds of seed appear, in a 3 : 1 split, and the new mixes, round-green and wrinkled-yellow, never show up.
Unglue them. Mendel called the full list of offspring kinds a combination series: the shape series and the colour series combined term by term.
Now Mendel's own seeds: 315, 101, 108 and 32 out of 556. They sit almost on top of the model. The mismatch is only about 1%, and chance pairing explains the rest.

understand.explanation: When a hybrid differs in two traits, shape and colour each split 3 : 1 as if the other trait were not there. A quarter of the seeds are wrinkled, and a quarter of the round ones and a quarter of the wrinkled ones are green, so the shares multiply into 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 out of 16. Mendel crossed round-yellow peas with wrinkled (he says 'angular') green ones. His 15 hybrid plants gave 556 seeds: 315 round yellow, 101 wrinkled yellow, 108 round green and 32 wrinkled green. That is close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 but not exact, because chance decides which pollen meets which egg. He then sowed the seeds and found nine kinds of breeding behaviour, exactly the list you get by combining the two single-trait series, and he got the same result with three traits at once. He showed this for the pea traits he tested; the paper does not claim that every pair of traits in every living thing behaves this way.
understand.quote: the offspring of the hybrids in which several essentially different characters are combined represent the terms of a series of combinations, in which the developmental series for each pair of differentiating characters are associated. It is demonstrated at the same time that the relation of each pair of different characters in hybrid union is independent of the other differences in the two original parental stocks.
understand.quote_where: Mendel, Experiments in Plant-Hybridisation: 'The Offspring of Hybrids in which Several Differentiating Characters are Associated'

connect.caption: This is the ratio as Bateson states it in his introduction. A is round and a is wrinkled; B is yellow and b is green. So AB is round-yellow, Ab round-green, aB wrinkled-yellow and ab wrinkled-green. Each coloured number is the matching 'out of 16' output, and it reads 9, 3, 3, 1 when each slider sits at the single-trait share of hidden-look seeds.

concepts.recap: Traits that sort independently multiply: ¾ × ¾, ¾ × ¼, ¼ × ¾ and ¼ × ¼ give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, and Mendel's 315 : 101 : 108 : 32 matches it closely.

activities.prompt: Mendel's 556 seeds from round-yellow × wrinkled-green hybrids. Match each count to the share the rule predicts for it. Remember that wrinkled and green are the hidden versions.

pairs.target: Both traits show the dominant look: 9 in 16 (about 313)
pairs.feedback: Round and yellow are both dominant, so this is ¾ × ¾ = 9/16. 556 × 9/16 ≈ 313, and Mendel counted 315.

pairs.target: Only shape shows the hidden look: 3 in 16 (about 104)
pairs.feedback: Wrinkled is hidden but yellow is dominant: ¼ × ¾ = 3/16 ≈ 104. Mendel counted 101.

pairs.target: Only colour shows the hidden look: 3 in 16 (about 104)
pairs.feedback: Round is dominant but green is hidden: ¾ × ¼ = 3/16 ≈ 104. Mendel counted 108.

pairs.target: Both traits show the hidden look: 1 in 16 (about 35)
pairs.feedback: Both hidden versions must turn up together: ¼ × ¼ = 1/16 ≈ 35. Mendel counted 32.

activities.takeaway: Every count sits within a few seeds of its predicted share. The small gaps are what chance pairing of pollen and egg leaves behind in a sample of 556.

concepts.title: Same ancestors, different futures: the 1902 dispute
concepts.idea: Because each germ cell is pure, a recessive pea pulled from a hybrid family breeds as true as one with no cross in its pedigree, so ancestry alone cannot predict offspring, as Bateson argued against Weldon.

terms.means: Galton's rule that an offspring's makeup comes about half from its parents, a quarter from its grandparents, an eighth from its great-grandparents, and so on
A single pollen grain or egg cell: the cells that join to start a new plant
A plant showing the hidden (recessive) trait that turns up among the offspring of a hybrid
Gives offspring that all show the same trait as itself, generation after generation

concepts.recap: Same family tree, different futures: what decides a plant's offspring is which pure germ cells met, which is why a trait can vanish for a generation and return unchanged in about one plant in four.

understand.explanation: In 1902 the biologist W. F. R. Weldon argued that to predict a plant's offspring you must know its whole family tree, following Galton's law of ancestral heredity: parents supply about half of an offspring's makeup, the four grandparents a quarter, the great-grandparents an eighth, and so on. William Bateson replied with Mendel's result that each germ cell (each pollen grain or egg) carries only one version of a trait, so a green pea that turns up among a hybrid's offspring, an extracted recessive, was made from two green germ cells and carries no yellow at all. It therefore breeds true, giving only green seeds just like a pea from a family that was always green, while its yellow-looking brothers and sisters, with exactly the same ancestors, may split again: same family tree, different futures. Bateson was writing as a committed defender: he admitted real exceptions, such as the irregular pea 'Telephone', and wrote that perfect purity of germ cells had not yet been proven for any case, so how far Mendel's rule reached was still an open question. But where the rule fits, it explains the whole story: a trait can vanish completely in one generation and return, unchanged, in almost exactly one plant out of four, because every pollen grain and egg carries only one version of the trait and chance pairing does the rest.
understand.quote: Of these the forms AA and BB, formed by the union of similar germs, are stated to be as pure as if they had had no cross in their pedigree, and henceforth their offspring will be no more likely to depart from the A type or the B type respectively, than those of any other originally pure specimens of these types.
understand.quote_where: A Defence of Mendel's Principles of Heredity, Section I (Bateson)

activities.question: A pea plant from a family that has only ever had yellow seeds is crossed with one from a family that has only ever had green seeds. The hybrid's own seeds include some green ones. You plant one of those green seeds and let it fertilise itself. What do you expect its seeds to be?

options.feedback: A bold guess. Keep it in mind: the next screens show what Mendel actually saw, and why it caused an argument.

options.text: Mostly green, but a few yellow, because a yellow grandparent is in the family
options.feedback: A natural guess, and close to how many biologists in 1902 reasoned. The next screens test it against Mendel's counts.

options.text: About half yellow and half green
options.feedback: This treats the green plant as if it still held yellow and green equally. The next screens look at what it really carries.

options.text: Impossible to say without the plant's full family tree
options.feedback: This is close to the position of the critic in this dispute. The next screens show why another biologist disagreed.

activities.prompt: Take the green pea from the first screen: its grandparents were one pure yellow and one pure green plant. What does each view of heredity expect from its seeds, and what did Mendel record?

cases.label: Family-tree view (Galton, Weldon)
cases.text: Its heritage comes partly from every ancestor, about a quarter from the grandparents, and one grandparent was yellow. So some yellow should keep turning up among its descendants, fading only slowly over the generations. Knowing the family tree is needed for a good prediction.

cases.label: Germ-cell view (Mendel, Bateson)
cases.text: It was made by one green pollen grain meeting one green egg. It carries no yellow version at all, so every germ cell it makes is green and all its seeds are green. The yellow grandparent makes no difference.

cases.label: What Mendel recorded
cases.text: Bateson summarises Mendel's peas: 'the offspring of the recessives remained pure recessive, and in subsequent generations never produced the dominant again.' Mendel followed his first two experiments through six generations and saw no departure from this.

activities.takeaway: The two views make different predictions for the same plant. In Mendel's peas the germ-cell view matched the counts: an extracted green pea bred as true as any green pea, whatever its grandparents were.

activities.title: Weldon, Bateson, or common ground?
activities.prompt: Sort each claim by who made it in the 1902 dispute, or put it in common ground if both sides accepted it.

cards.text: A plant's offspring depend on all its ancestors, not only on its two parents.
cards.feedback: Weldon. He wrote that the condition of an animal depends 'upon the condition of all its ancestors in every past generation', following Galton and Pearson.

cards.text: The fundamental mistake of work based on Mendel's method is the neglect of ancestry.
cards.feedback: Weldon, almost word for word. Bateson quoted it in order to attack it.

cards.text: Mendel's yellow crosses came from 58 flowers on ten plants, so they cannot settle how yellow and green peas of any family behave.
cards.feedback: Weldon. It is a fair point about sample size. Bateson's reply was that Mendel never claimed a rule for all peas of every family.

cards.text: A green pea pulled from a hybrid family is as pure as one with no cross in its family tree.
cards.feedback: Bateson, stating Mendel's principle: forms made by the union of similar germ cells are 'as pure as if they had had no cross in their pedigree'.

cards.text: Brothers and sisters with exactly the same ancestors can produce completely different offspring.
cards.feedback: Bateson: 'the same ancestry is common to own brothers and sisters endowed with dissimilar properties and producing dissimilar posterity.' An extracted green and a hybrid yellow are such siblings.

cards.text: Saying 'ancestry explains it' without saying how is just a way of saying we do not know.
cards.feedback: Bateson. He called Weldon's appeal to unknown pedigrees 'simply an appeal to ignorance'.

cards.text: Yellow does not beat green in every cross: some varieties, such as Telephone, behave irregularly.
cards.feedback: Common ground. Weldon stressed these exceptions, and Bateson accepted that a few were real while arguing that they do not overturn germ-cell purity.

cards.text: Mendel's own counts in his peas are not in doubt.
cards.feedback: Common ground. Bateson noted that Weldon 'is careful nowhere directly to question Mendel's facts'. They disagreed about what the facts meant and how far they reach.

activities.takeaway: Both sides accepted Mendel's counts and accepted that exceptions exist. They disagreed about the cause: Weldon pointed to the family tree, while Bateson pointed to which pure germ cells met.

activities.question: Back to your first guess. Two green peas grow side by side. One comes from a family that has been green for a hundred years. The other was pulled last year from the offspring of a yellow × green hybrid. Each fertilises itself. On Mendel's results as Bateson presents them, what should you expect?

options.text: Both give only green seeds, and the recent cross in one family tree makes no difference
options.feedback: Supported. Each plant was formed from two green germ cells, so neither carries a yellow version to pass on. This is Mendel's observation that extracted recessives 'remained pure'. The caveat is Bateson's own: he said absolute purity had not been proven universally, and odd varieties like Telephone exist.

options.text: The hybrid-family pea throws some yellow seeds, because it has a yellow grandparent
options.feedback: This is the family-tree prediction. In Mendel's peas, green plants pulled from hybrids never produced yellow again over several generations. The yellow grandparent's version went into other germ cells, not this plant.

options.text: The old-family pea is purer and gives fewer stray yellows
options.feedback: The length of a family tree does not add purity. Bateson argued that the number of generations a trait has stayed pure changes nothing, so long as the plant's germ cells all carry the same version.

options.text: Neither can be predicted without both full family trees
options.feedback: This is Weldon's position. Bateson's point is that the family tree is not needed here: what matters is that both plants are made of two green germ cells, which their green seeds already show.

hints: Ask what kind of germ cells must have met to make a green (recessive) pea.
Could a plant made from two green germ cells hold a yellow version to hand on?
